title: The evening review
hook: Seneca's three questions or Ignatius' gratitude
tomorrow: a monk hears one verse, says 'enough for now,' and leaves. why?

segments.voice: That was a week through the day's hours: my morning, noon, the food arrived, between, the heavy hour, and yesterday, the day turns, a lamp lit at dusk. One thing is left before sleep: looking back.
screen: `THE DAY TURNS.` → `A WEEK THROUGH THE HOURS.`

segments.voice: Lying in bed replaying every awkward thing you said today is its own kind of trial, with no judge and no verdict. Seneca, a Roman Stoic, held a real one. In his book On Anger he writes that when the lamp has been taken away, and his wife, who knows his habit, has gone quiet, he examines his whole day and goes back over what he did and said. He hides nothing from himself. He passes nothing over.
screen: `A TRIAL WITH NO VERDICT.` → `THE LAMP TAKEN AWAY.` → `HE HIDES NOTHING FROM HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: He learned it from the philosopher Sextius, who asked himself every night: what bad habit have I cured today? What fault have I resisted? In what way am I better? Then Seneca reads out his own charges. In that argument, you spoke too sharply. With that man, you corrected him so bluntly that you offended him instead of helping. And then the verdict, which is the surprise: see that you don't do that again; this time I pardon you. That's the teaching, the Stoic evening review: an honest court, held every night, that ends in pardon rather than punishment. Seneca says the sleep that follows is sweeter. Christians keep an evening review of their own, in their own words. Ignatius of Loyola taught the Examen, a prayer looking back over the day that begins not with faults but with thanks for the day's gifts, and only then asks what went wrong. Two ways of looking back, each from its own house: Seneca's three questions, or Ignatius's gratitude first. Either way, the day gets looked at once, honestly, and then put down.
screen: `WHAT HABIT HAVE I CURED TODAY?` · `THE CHARGES, READ PLAINLY.` · `THIS TIME I PARDON YOU.` · `OR IGNATIUS: THANKS FIRST.` · then, large: `THE REVIEW.`

segments.voice: Open your notebook and write three short lines about today: one thing you're thankful for, one thing you'd do differently, and one word of pardon to yourself, the way Seneca ended his court. Keep each line plain and true. Then close the notebook; the day has been looked at, and can be put down.
The evening review: looking back over the day honestly, once, before sleep. Seneca's nightly court; Ignatius's Examen.
Your line: the review. An honest court that ends in pardon, or thanks that comes first. Two weeks of the daily practice, done.

chat.meaning: Seneca examined his day each night, named his faults plainly, and ended: this time I pardon you. A review is a court that ends in pardon.

tie.story: Each night, with the lamp out, Seneca went over his day, named what he'd done wrong, and pardoned himself this time.

Seneca.meaning: a Roman Stoic philosopher, writer and statesman

Sextius.meaning: a Roman philosopher who questioned himself every night

Ignatius of Loyola.meaning: a Spanish priest who founded the Jesuits and taught the Examen

Examen.meaning: a Christian prayer looking back over the day, thanks first
